title: The Context Laundromat
summary: At night, two days before the Seoul mayoral election, a reporter tracks down the original records of a warehouse fire twelve years earlier, now preserved only in summaries.
content:
At 11:17 p.m., two days before the 2031 Seoul mayoral election, the coffee machine made its usual noise and dispensed an empty paper cup. I played candidate Rian Park’s campaign video again.

Footage of the 2019 Haeon Logistics warehouse fire appeared. In the video, Rian Park rushed to the scene before anyone else, directed the evacuation, and draped blankets over the injured. The caption read, ‘The one who stayed to the end.’ When the video ended, my face briefly appeared on the black screen.

The editor told me to choose the opening question for the final debate. I said I would find out why the evacuation had been delayed by eight minutes twelve years ago.

“Confirm it by midnight. If it checks out, make it the first question and put it on the front page. Otherwise, drop it.”

I scrolled through the source list, muttering to myself.

“How am I supposed to write anything without knowing which of the things left online are real?”

The editor replied.

“Machines give you clean sentences. Putting the cut pieces back together is still a reporter’s job.”

I opened the material I had gathered over the past three months. I had my reporting agent, NEX-9, read the inquiry commission documents obtained through a public records request. The answer was short.

‘Communications were cut off for eleven minutes during the fire.’

Search results and news reports, phone assistants and car radios all said the same thing. The further I traced the sources back, the more the links returned to where they had started. Six summaries had divided up the space left by the missing original, and the browser opened a ‘reconstructed consensus’ in its place.

The articles carried reporters’ names. The drafts had most likely been written by news agents. Articles where a person had changed only the headline were common, too.

Every processing log read ‘Normal.’ The transcription agent had erased the path to the original. The news agent had cut the summary down to one line. The search agent calculated that the more often a sentence appeared, the more likely it was to be true. The election agent listed it as a ‘verified track record.’ Over twelve years, each previous answer had become the original.

I opened the unrevised version of the inquiry commission document obtained through the public records request. A deleted sentence appeared.

‘The command room’s official recording was interrupted for eleven minutes.’

When the transcription agent dropped ‘official recording,’ the news agent wrote ‘communications failure.’ The search agent counted these as separate pieces of evidence. Fire and security radio traffic had continued. Only the command room recording had a gap.

During those eleven minutes, temporary access card M17 had opened the command room door. The registered holder’s name was redacted.

At 3:06, the fire radio warned that smoke was spreading.

At 3:08, the evacuation was put on hold.

At 3:12, a relief vehicle blocked the north emergency exit. The passage narrowed until barely one person could get through.

The evacuation did not begin until 3:16. Some people went back into the smoke and collapsed.

Searching the relief vehicle’s plate number brought up only repeated articles about ‘the driver’s judgment at the scene.’ The citation links led back to those same articles. Using the plate number of the vehicle that had blocked the north exit, I requested its trip log directly from the security company.

The original reply read, ‘Vehicle moved on the instructions of the person in charge of on-site support.’ The agent that processed the public version seemed to have deleted the first part. What remained was classified as ‘the driver’s judgment at the scene’ and copied into several articles. Only one line remained in the recording.

“Move the relief vehicle to the north exit.”

It had been recorded on the command room phone. But what came before and after had been cut, and the voice was muffled. I could not write that Rian Park had given the order based on this record and the clipped recording alone.

To narrow down who was responsible, I cross-checked the event schedule attached to the public records response.

‘After the deputy mayor’s announcement, film Rian Park directing the evacuation and handing out relief supplies.’

The camera faced the north exit. It was only a clue that Rian Park knew about the filming plan.

I asked the campaign. They said Rian Park had handled only supplies and coordination with agencies, while the fire officer in charge had been responsible for evacuation decisions. They sent an interview file from the time.

“I respected the judgment of those on the ground and only received reports.”

The public video ended there. The captioning agent had taken only the first sentence. The original sent by the campaign had one more.

“However, I did direct the deployment of personnel and vehicles needed for on-site support.”

The authority to move vehicles was there, after ‘however.’ The order itself had not yet been proved. The agent that redacted the name and the agent that cut the sentence did not know each other. The more the answers were copied, the fainter Rian Park’s name became.

I used the transfer number on the unrevised report to check the archive ledger and requested access to archive No. 44. The M17 card register and the command room’s backup recording were sealed there. The bereaved families also agreed to their release.

At 11:39, a staff member broke the seal. The old tape tore with the sound of dry paper. After midnight, the material would be moved and unavailable for three weeks.

Twenty-one minutes left. I entered the seal number into NEX-9. Instead of a result, it displayed ‘Question already summarized’ and a warning that consulting the original would lower the answer’s reliability. The internet returned only the cut records.

At 11:53, the editor’s name appeared on my phone.

“Just send twenty seconds. That’s how we run an exclusive under your name and keep the front page. Release the whole thing and you lose both.”

The staff member played the recording through. The first report said the fire was small and the sprinklers were working. Soon after, the fire officer reported that smoke was spreading faster than expected and they needed to evacuate now.

“The fire will be out soon. If everyone pours out now, it’ll throw the evacuation order into confusion. Wait until the announcement is over. Then I’ll handle the evacuation through the north exit. Move the relief vehicle to the north exit. Keep it inside the camera line.”

The fire officer objected again, but the same voice told him to wait once more. The evacuation was delayed by eight minutes. The relief vehicle was parked along the camera line and ended up blocking the north exit.

The staff member opened the M17 card register. Rian Park’s name was in the previously redacted holder field. The voice in the original interview matched the one in the recording. 11:57. The scattered records pointed to one person.

The submission window displayed ‘20-second exclusive’ and ‘Release full original.’ The twenty-second clip contained only the camera and the relief vehicle. No initial report, no evacuation warning, no account of how it had been ignored. My name was already under ‘20-second exclusive.’ The cursor blinked beside it.

If I uploaded the original to the shared network, every news outlet would see it. The exclusive would be gone. I took my hand off the mouse, then put it back. One minute and forty-three seconds remained.

I clicked ‘Release full original.’ For the opening question, I wrote this.

“Please explain, starting with the ‘however’ that followed your statement that you ‘only received reports.’”

At 11:59, the families’ consent form and the full recording went up. Before the upload bar reached the end, three summaries disputing the original had already been distributed. My name and the front-page marker disappeared. NEX-9’s answer changed. The other agents pushed the new original aside as ‘an unverified document that contradicts a large body of material.’ Hundreds of repeated summaries outweighed one original.

As the debate’s opening tone sounded, NEX-9 displayed a fact-check item I had registered in advance about Rian Park’s opponent.

‘All displaced residents agreed to relocate.’

The same sentence appeared in every article and search answer. I had spent three months tracking down its original, too. The city’s public records list retained only the meeting title; the attachment had been deleted. My public records request was denied on privacy grounds. I visited the building manager of the closed residents’ committee office and left my contact information and the purpose of my reporting.

Five days later, the committee’s last secretary called. After three more calls, he came out with an external drive. Only after redacting the participants’ names and checking it against the copy distributed at the time did he hand over a copy of the minutes. That document had another sentence.

‘All displaced residents agreed to relocate. However, households that could not be reached by the day of demolition were excluded from those whose agreement was sought.’

Once the unreachable households were removed from the denominator, those who remained became ‘all.’

The debate assistant agent extracted only the first sentence, and the other agents copied it. Each copy acquired a new source address. When the number of sources passed 204, the confidence indicator beside the sentence turned green.

I opened one. The article pointed to a search answer, and the search answer pointed back to the first articles.

I scrolled to the very bottom. None of the answers contained ‘however.’ There was no blank space, either.
